You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis
Details: 
- What the test does:
  - MinpackTest.minpackTest creates a LevenbergMarquardtOptimizer, sets strict LM-specific tolerances (costRelativeTolerance ≈ sqrt(machine epsilon), parRelativeTolerance ≈ sqrt(machine epsilon), orthoTolerance ≈ machine epsilon), and calls optimize with the Jennrich-Sampson problem (2 parameters, 10 residuals). It expects convergence to the known minimum near [0.2578330049, 0.257829976764542] without throwing an exception.

- Expected behavior from the optimizer:
  - AbstractLeastSquaresOptimizer’s constructor installs a VectorialConvergenceChecker (by default, SimpleVectorialValueChecker). Callers can also set their own checker. The optimizer should consult this checker each iteration to decide when to stop based on user-specified criteria (e.g., changes in parameters and/or residuals), providing flexible stopping conditions.

- What actually happens in the code:
  - AbstractLeastSquaresOptimizer.optimize sets up the problem and delegates to LevenbergMarquardtOptimizer.doOptimize.
  - Inside LevenbergMarquardtOptimizer.doOptimize, all convergence decisions are made using hard-coded Levenberg–Marquardt criteria:
    - An outer-loop early exit if the orthogonality measure maxCosine <= orthoTolerance.
    - In the inner loop, convergence is decided only by LM-specific thresholds: |actRed| <= costRelativeTolerance, preRed <= costRelativeTolerance, ratio <= 2.0, or delta <= parRelativeTolerance * xNorm.
    - If these are not satisfied, the code may eventually throw exceptions about too-small tolerances or continue iterating until the iteration limit is reached.
  - Critically, the code never calls or references the VectorialConvergenceChecker that was configured in AbstractLeastSquaresOptimizer. There is even a misleading comment “we use the vectorial convergence checker” right above the block that uses only the LM-specific tolerances, confirming the intention but not the implementation.

- Why this causes the failure:
  - Because the LevenbergMarquardtOptimizer ignores the configured VectorialConvergenceChecker, stopping is governed solely by LM-internal tolerances. For the Jennrich–Sampson case with very strict tolerances, this can lead to either:
    - Running more iterations than necessary (since a checker would typically stop once successive parameter/value changes are sufficiently small), risking hitting the max-iterations limit, or
    - Different termination behavior than what the default/custom checker would trigger, potentially leading to a different final point or an exception.
  - The test expects clean convergence to the known minimum without exceptions. With the checker ignored, the optimizer’s termination conditions diverge from the intended/customizable criteria, leading to the observed failure.

In short: The root cause is that LevenbergMarquardtOptimizer.doOptimize never invokes the VectorialConvergenceChecker provided via AbstractLeastSquaresOptimizer; it uses hard-coded LM tolerances instead. This mismatch in stopping logic explains the failure in the Jennrich–Sampson Minpack test and matches the issue report that custom stopping criteria are ignored.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
